title: Queen mate in a few moves
summary: King and queen against king: the two mates, the box, the king that comes, the waiting move and the mate without stalemate.
part.box.title: The box
part.box.summary: The queen a knight's jump away, without check, traps the black king and shrinks the box.
step.t_seirawan: In chapter 4 the king got into the box. Now: when should the queen stop. Seirawan's example again, after 1.Qf6 Kd5 2.Qe7 Kd4. The queen holds the black king on the a- to d-files, below the seventh. What is the next step?
step.t_seirawan.hint1: Does one more queen move shrink the box? And who is needed for the mate?
step.goal: This is the first picture, the support mate: the queen right next to the black king, on e7, taking d8, f8, d7 and f7. He cannot take her because my king protects her. Here my king stands in front, on e6, but it would also protect e7 from d6 or f6, the two squares a knight's jump from e8.
step.edge: The second picture, the edge mate, as the books show it: the kings face to face, mine on e6 and Black's on e8, and the queen checks from far away along the eighth rank. My king takes d7, e7 and f7; the queen, the whole rank. Opposition is not required: it is enough that king and queen together cover every square.
step.jump: To push the black king, the queen does not need to give check. Put her a knight's jump away from the king, like here: king on e5, queen on f3. She becomes two walls, the f-file and the third rank, and the king is shut inside a rectangle, the box. A check only pushes the king from one side to the other; a wall takes squares away for good. So the plan has two parts: drive the black king to the edge with the box, and bring my king.
step.follow: Your turn, with the queen only. After each move of the black king, put the queen a knight's jump from him again, so that the box gets smaller.
step.follow.hint: Count the knight's jump from the black king and pick the square that shrinks his box. No checks.
step.follow.done: Knight's jumps, no checks, and the box got smaller with every move. Notice that your king is still on a1: in the next chapter it comes in.
step.t_corner: So far, every wall helped. On the edge, one wall too many draws. The black king is in the corner and the queen is very close to it. Is this good for White? Count Black's moves.
step.t_corner.hint1: Look at each square next to the black king and who guards it. And check whether it is in check.
step.stop: The queen has done her part: she closes the e-file and the seventh rank. One more knight's jump, 1.Qe6, squeezes a little, but it costs a move, because without my king there is no mate. So the queen stops and my king comes, even with the black king still far from the edge. Do not wait for the edge to bring the king.
step.stalemate: Black has no move and is not in check: stalemate, a draw. The queen on c7 takes a7, b7 and b8 without touching the king. The same happens with the queen on b6, a knight's jump from a8. On the edge, the knight's jump is no longer the rule: before every queen move, count the black king's squares. At least one, or check.
step.bring: The black king is stuck between g8 and h8, and the queen on e7 closes the seventh rank. Bring your king and mate when it arrives. There are stalemates on the way: 1.Qf7, right now, would be the first.
step.bring.hint: The queen has done her job; leave her where she is. Walk your king up the g-file to the sixth rank, next to the black king.
step.bring.done: Mate. Notice that 4.Qf6, on the last move, would also have been stalemate: the black king with no square and no check. The queen stayed put, the king came, and only then the blow.
step.recap: Three rules to take with you. First: the queen a knight's jump from the black king, on your king's side, shrinking the box with no pointless checks. Second: once the black king is trapped, the queen stops and the king comes, without waiting for the edge; near the mate, a waiting move forces the black king to walk. Third: before every queen move, count the black king's squares; zero squares and no check is a draw.
step.finish: Now play until mate, from the middle of the board. The box on your king's side, the king that comes, and the mate. Count the black king's squares before every queen move.
ex.e05: The black king is on the edge, but there is no mate yet. Make him walk into it.
ex.e05.hint: One queen move, no check, that leaves the black king a single square. After that the mate comes by itself.
ex.e05.solution: 1.Qc7! closes the seventh rank and takes d8. The black king only has f8, and then comes 2.Qf7#, protected by the king, or 2.Qd8#, along the rank. Sometimes the strongest move is the one that threatens nothing: it forces the other side to move.
ex.e10: The black king is near the corner. Careful: there are two stalemates on the way. Find the winning move.
ex.e10.hint: First, the queen a knight's jump away, leaving the black king a single square. Then the king comes, and the mate has several forms.
ex.e10.solution: 1.Qe4! and the black king only has h3. 2.Kf2 (2.Qg6 also works) and the king goes to h2. Now 3.Qg2#, 3.Qh4# or 3.Qh7#. The traps: 2.Qf4? on the second move, the knight's jump from h3, is stalemate; and so is 3.Qf3? on the last one.
ex.e11: Your king is not in front of the black king: it is a knight's jump away from it. Find the mate.
ex.e11.hint: The queen can stand right next to the black king if your king protects her. Look for the square touching him that your king reaches.
ex.e11.solution: 1.Qd2#. The queen touches the black king and the king on c3 protects her; she takes c1, e1 and e2 herself, and the white king takes c2. Careful with 1.Qe3? It is the knight's jump from d1, it takes every square without giving check, and the black king is stalemated.
ex.e12: Again the kings are not face to face, and there are many checks on the board. Only one is mate. Find the mate.
ex.e12.hint: Your king already takes e2 and f2. You need a check from afar, along the first rank, that also watches the square left on the second.
ex.e12.solution: 1.Qh1#. The queen checks along the first rank and, from the corner, also watches g2 on the diagonal; the king on e3 takes e2 and f2. 1.Qf3+ or 1.Qd1+ leave an escape, and 1.Qg2+? gives the queen away. The edge mate does not need the kings in opposition: king and queen together just have to cover every square.
ex.e13: The queen already holds the black king on the first three ranks. What is faster: squeeze harder with the queen, or bring the king? Find the winning move.
ex.e13.hint: The queen cannot mate alone. Think about which piece is missing to close the other side of the box.
ex.e13.solution: 1.Ke2! The white king becomes the wall on the f-file: the black king only has g2, h2 and h3, and the queen comes in for the blow. The knight's jump 1.Qe4 also holds, but costs two more moves, and sliding the queen along the fourth rank with 1.Qf4+?, 1.Qg4+? or 1.Qh4+? gives her away. When the box is already small, the king does the work.
ex.e14: The black king is in the center and your pieces are in the corner. Only one queen move keeps the fastest path. Then keep going. Find the winning move.
ex.e14.hint: There is more than one knight's jump. Pick the box that pushes the black king towards your king, not away from it.
ex.e14.solution: 1.Qe7!, a knight's jump from d5: the walls are the e-file and the seventh rank, and the black king stays on the side of the board where your king is. 1.Qe3, the other knight's jump, closes the box on the wrong side, far from the white king, and costs two moves; 1.Qc5+? and 1.Qd6+? give the queen away. After 1...Kc6 the queen has done her part: 2.Kb2 or 2.Ka2, and the king comes.
ex.e15: The black king is close, but nothing is obvious: the fastest path has a single move almost every turn. Find them, and do not stalemate at the end.
ex.e15.hint: First, a queen wall that leaves your king on the inside, already near the black king. Then the king climbs right next to him, and the queen just waits.
ex.e15.solution: 1.Qg4! closes the fourth rank and the g-file with your king inside the box (1.Qg5 also holds, but costs two moves; 1.Qe3+? and 1.Qd4+? give the queen away). After 1...Ke3, 2.Kc2! takes d2 and d3, and the black king must go to f2. 3.Kd2 (or 3.Kd3) and 3...Kf1, then 4.Ke3! steps up close, taking e2 and f2: 4...Ke1 is forced, and 5.Qg1# or 5.Qe2# follows. The trap is on the fourth move: 4.Qg3? takes every square without check and stalemates.
key.supportMate: The simplest mate: the queen sits right next to the black king, protected by her own king.
key.edgeMate: The black king on the edge and the white king facing it: the queen checks along the whole rank, and it's mate.
key.knightJump: The queen stands a knight's jump from the black king: without checking, she traps it in a box that only gets smaller.
key.cornerStalemate: The most common trap: the black king in the corner, not in check and with no move at all. That's stalemate, and the win becomes a draw.
key.seirawan: The black king in the middle of the board and the white pieces in the corner: the queen builds the box, the white king comes to help, and the mate comes easily.
key.lichessPractice: King and queen in the centre against the lone king: the same recipe, push it to the edge and bring the king over for the mate.
history: King and queen against king is the first mate everyone learns, and the one that turns up most: nearly every pawn that promotes leads to it. With a queen the mate always comes, and in a few moves. The real danger is something else: stalemating the enemy king and throwing away a won game, a mistake made at every level. A curiosity: for centuries the piece beside the king moved only one square diagonally, and this mate was hard work. The queen got her modern move in Spain at the end of the fifteenth century, and one of the first books to teach it was by Luis Ramírez de Lucena, the same Lucena who gives this app its name.
practice: Now the real ending: king on c2, queen on c1, and the black king on d7. Box, edge, king and mate, without stalemate. Choose the time control and go.
part.support.title: The support mate
part.support.summary: The queen sits next to the black king and your king protects her, from in front or from the side.
part.edge.title: The edge mate
part.edge.summary: The check comes from far away; the kings do not need to face each other.
part.side.title: The side of the box
part.side.summary: Between two knight's jumps, the one that leaves your king on the inside.
part.king.title: The queen stops, the king comes
part.king.summary: Once the black king is trapped, the king does the work, even far from the edge.
part.wait.title: The waiting move
part.wait.summary: A move without check that leaves the black king a single square.
part.stalemate.title: No stalemate
part.stalemate.summary: Count the black king's squares before every queen move.
step.t_support: I start from the end, because it helps to know where you are going. The black king is on the edge and the queen already closes the seventh rank. What is the fastest way to mate?
step.t_support.hint1: The queen alone cannot mate right next to the black king: she needs a guard.
step.t_support.hint2: Your king does not have to stand in front of the black king to protect the queen.
step.d_support: Back to the starting position. The answer, move by move.
step.d_support.m1: 1.Kd6. The king comes to d6, a knight's jump from e8, the only square the black king will have left, and already protects e7. The black king, held on the eighth rank by the queen, has only e8.
step.d_support.m2: 1...Ke8. It is the only move: c8 belongs to the queen, and c7, d7 and e7 to my king and the queen.
step.d_support.m3: 2.Qe7, mate. The queen sits next to the black king, protected by the king on d6, and takes d8, f8, d7 and f7. My king is not in front, and it is mate all the same.
step.supportMove: Now on another edge, the a-file. Your king is already a knight's jump from the black king. Give mate.
step.supportMove.hint: Look for the square next to the black king that your king protects.
step.supportMove.done: Mate. The queen on b5 is protected by the king on c6 and takes every square from the black king. Beware of 1.Qc4? It also takes every square, but without check, and that is stalemate.
step.t_nakamura: In chapter 1 the queen sat next to the black king. Now she mates from far away. This is Nakamura, with White, against Abarca Gonzalez, in an online blitz event in 2022. There are several mates here. Find one where the queen does not touch the black king.
step.t_nakamura.hint1: The king on f7 already takes g8 and g7.
step.t_nakamura.hint2: What is missing is a check along the h-file.
step.d_nakamura: How Nakamura got there. He gave his rook for Abarca Gonzalez's knight, promoted the e-pawn and, with the new queen, drove the black king into the corner. We go back four half-moves.
step.d_nakamura.m1: 90.Qg5. Without check, the queen closes the g-file; the black king is stuck on h8 and h7. 90.Kf7 at once was one move faster.
step.d_nakamura.m2: 90...Kh7. It is the only move: g8 and g7 are on the queen's file.
step.d_nakamura.m3: 91.Kf7. The king does not go in front of the black king: it goes to f7, and from there it takes g8, g7 and g6. With h6 guarded by the queen, the black king can only go back to the corner.
step.d_nakamura.m4: 91...Kh8. Forced: h6 belongs to the queen, and g6, g7 and g8 to my king.
step.d_nakamura.m5: 92.Qh4, mate, Nakamura's move. The check comes from far away along the h-file, which also takes h7; the king on f7 covers g7 and g8. The kings are not face to face, and it is mate.
step.edgeMove: Your turn. There are nine checks in this position and only one is mate.
step.edgeMove.hint: Your king already takes g4 and g5. Which long-range check also guards g6?
step.edgeMove.done: Mate. From h7 the queen checks along the h-file and still hits g6 on the diagonal. The kings are not facing each other: count the squares, not the opposition.
step.t_box: Both mates only exist on the edge. Now: how to drive the black king there. Your king is far away, in the corner. With one queen move, without check, trap the black king in the smallest space you can.
step.t_box.hint1: A check only pushes the king; a wall takes squares away for good.
step.t_box.hint2: Count the squares a knight's jump from the black king that the queen can reach.
step.d_box: Back to the starting position. The answer, move by move.
step.d_box.m1: 1.Qe6, a knight's jump from d4. The queen becomes two walls, the e-file and the sixth rank: the black king is held on the a- to d-files, below the sixth, without a single check.
step.d_box.m2: 1...Kc5. The black king heads where there is more room, away from both walls.
step.d_box.m3: 2.Qe4, another knight's jump, now from c5. The rank wall moves from the sixth to the fourth, now below the black king: he can no longer go down, and the box has shrunk.
step.d_box.m4: 2...Kb6. He moves away from the queen, towards the upper corner, where there is still room.
step.d_box.m5: 3.Qc4, a knight's jump from b6. Now the walls are the c-file and the fourth rank: the black king is held on the a- and b-files, above the fourth.
step.d_box.m6: 3...Kb7. There is no way out: the c-file and the fourth rank belong to the queen, and he can only walk inside the small box.
step.t_carlsen: In chapter 3 your king stayed still. In a game, it has to get into the box. This is the ending of Carlsen against Anand, at the Glitnir Blitz in Reykjavik, 2006: Carlsen gave his rook for Anand's e-pawn, his d-pawn queened, and the white king also took the h-pawn. White to play. Only one queen move keeps the shortest path. Which one?
step.t_carlsen.hint1: The black king is on e3. Count the squares a knight's jump from it that the queen can reach.
step.t_carlsen.hint2: In which of them does the wall leave the black king on the same side as your king?
step.t_carlsen.hint3: Your king, on g3, has to stay on the inside of the box, close to the black king.
step.side: In the example from Seirawan's book, with the black king on e4 and White in the corner, the queen can reach two knight's jumps: f6 and c3. 1.Qf6 closes the f-file and the sixth rank, and the black king stays below, on the side of my king on b1. 1.Qc3 closes the c-file and the third rank, and the black king stays above, far from my king: the mate comes two moves later. Choose the box that leaves the black king between your king and the wall.
step.d_carlsen: What Carlsen played, up to the mate.
step.d_carlsen.m1: 75.Qd5! A knight's jump from e3: the walls are the d-file and the fifth rank, and the king on g3 stays on the inside, two squares from the black king.
step.d_carlsen.m2: 75...Ke2. It is the only move: d2, d3 and d4 belong to the queen, e4 is on her diagonal, and f2, f3 and f4 belong to my king.
step.d_carlsen.m3: 76.Qd4! Another knight's jump, now from e2. The wall drops to the fourth rank, and the diagonal takes e3: the black king has only e1 and f1, on the edge.
step.d_carlsen.m4: 76...Ke1. The black king has only e1 and f1; Anand picks e1, because on f1 mate would come at once, with 77.Qf2 or 77.Qd1.
step.d_carlsen.m5: 77.Kf3! The queen has stopped: the black king is already on the edge, and now the king takes the squares. From f3 it covers e2, f2 and g2.
step.d_carlsen.m6: 77...Kf1. It is the only move: d1 and d2 belong to the queen, and e2 and f2 to my king.
step.d_carlsen.m7: 78.Qd1, mate, and that is how the game ended. It is the second picture: kings face to face, f3 against f1, and the long-range check along the first rank.
step.sideMove: Your turn. Choose the knight's jump on your king's side, then bring the king.
step.sideMove.hint: Your king is on g2. The good box leaves the black king between your king and the wall.
step.sideMove.done: That's it. 1.Qe6 closes the e-file and the sixth rank with your king on the inside, and the king stepped up right next to the black king. 1.Qe2, the other jump, would leave your king outside and cost three moves.
step.t_seirawan.hint2: Who can take squares from the black king without giving check or stalemating?
step.d_seirawan: The king walks up, and the queen waits.
step.d_seirawan.m1: 1.Kc2. The king walks up the c-file, on the inside of the box, towards the black king.
step.d_seirawan.m2: 1...Kd5. The black king tries to stay in the centre, away from the edge and from my king.
step.d_seirawan.m3: 2.Kc3. My king takes c4 and d4, and the queen, on the diagonal, takes c5 and d6: the black king has only c6.
step.d_seirawan.m4: 2...Kc6. Forced: it is the only square the queen and my king left free.
step.d_seirawan.m5: 3.Kc4. My king takes b5, c5 and d5: the black king has only b6, near the edge.
step.d_seirawan.m6: 3...Kb6. Forced; the black king was pushed by my king, not by the queen.
step.d_seirawan.m7: 4.Qd7! Only now does the queen move, a knight's jump from b6: with my king on c4, the black king has only a5 and a6, on the edge.
step.kingMove: Your turn. The queen on a5 holds the black king below the fifth rank. Play the fastest moves.
step.kingMove.hint: The queen alone does not close the other side of the box.
step.kingMove.done: 1.Ke3 and then 2.Kd3 (or 2.Kd4): the king became the wall on the other side, and the black king is trapped in the lower corner. On the first move, every queen move cost at least two moves, and the close checks gave the queen away.
step.t_ding: In chapter 5 the king worked and the queen waited, standing still. Sometimes the queen waits by moving. Ding Liren against Le Quang Liem, 2017: both sides queened, the queens were traded, and Ding's b-pawn queened again. The black king is on g8. What is the fastest move?
step.t_ding.hint1: A check only pushes the king to another free square.
step.t_ding.hint2: Look for a move without check that leaves the black king a single square.
step.wait: Around the black king there are five squares, f8, f7, g7, h7 and h8, and the queen on f6 already takes four: h7 is left. The queen has to move without losing that. A check takes some squares and gives others back. The good move threatens nothing: it takes everything but one square, and the black king, who must move, has to go there. It is the waiting move.
step.d_ding.m1: 65.Qe7! No check. From e7 the queen hits f8, f7, g7 and h7: only h8 is left.
step.d_ding.m2: 65...Kh8. Forced: it is the only square the queen left, and passing is not allowed.
step.d_ding.m3: 66.Kf6! The king comes close, also without check, and protects g7. The black king has only g8.
step.d_ding.m4: 66...Kg8. It is the only move; in the game, Le Quang Liem resigned before playing it, because the mate is certain.
step.d_ding.m5: 67.Qg7, mate. The queen sits next to the black king, protected by the king on f6: the support mate from chapter 1.
step.waitMove: Your turn. With one queen move, without check, leave the black king a single square, and then give mate.
step.waitMove.hint: Which squares does the black king have now? Leave only one.
step.waitMove.done: 1.Qf6 closes the f-file and leaves the black king only d1, facing your king. Then, mate along the first rank. A check, such as 1.Qa1+, would cost four moves.
step.t_corner.hint2: Count the squares a7, b7 and b8.
step.d_andreikin: Nakamura against Andreikin, another online blitz event, in 2022. Nakamura queened the g-pawn and, with two queen moves, trapped the black king in the corner. The queen on d2 leaves it a1 and b1: always one square, never stalemate.
step.d_andreikin.m1: 68.Ke5. The queen does not move, because the box is done. The white king comes along the diagonal, the shortest way to c3.
step.d_andreikin.m2: 68...Ka1. The black king shuttles between a1 and b1, which is all it has. Careful now: 69.Qc2? would take b1 without check, and that would be stalemate.
step.d_andreikin.m3: 69.Kd4. The king keeps going along the diagonal, towards c3, the square that protects b2.
step.d_andreikin.m4: 69...Kb1. Again the only square: the queen still takes a2, b2, c1 and c2.
step.d_andreikin.m5: 70.Kc3. The king arrives and protects b2 and c2, the squares where the queen can sit next to the black king.
step.d_andreikin.m6: 70...Ka1. Forced: a1 is the only free square, and the black king goes back to the corner.
step.d_andreikin.m7: 71.Qb2, mate, as Nakamura played. The queen sits next to the black king, protected by the king on c3: the support mate, in the corner.
key.carlsenAnand: Carlsen against Anand, Glitnir Blitz, Reykjavik, 2006: Qd5!, the knight's jump that keeps the white king inside the box, and mate on d1.
key.dingLe: Ding Liren against Le Quang Liem, Huai'an, 2017: Qe7!, the waiting move, and Black resigned after Kf6.
